turns.speaker: Skeptic
turns.style: cocky, relaxed, amused; unhurried opening, dismissive scoff before 'Easy'
turns.text: T. rex versus Triceratops? <pff> Easy. That's just lunch.

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.style: calm, dry, quietly intrigued; slows down to show the fossil
turns.text: Is it? <short pause> Look at this. A Triceratops horn... with T. rex tooth marks. And the bone grew back. It healed. This Triceratops survived.

turns.speaker: Skeptic
turns.text: <gasp> Survived a T. rex?! Twelve meters, and the strongest bite of any known land animal?

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.style: confident, brisk list delivery, each number landing with weight
turns.text: True. But Triceratops was no snack. Nine meters, up to twelve tons, a two-and-a-half-meter skull, and horns a meter long.

turns.speaker: Skeptic
turns.text: So? Sneak around and bite the neck.

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.style: lowered voice, intent, clear; slight pause for effect
turns.text: The bite's on the horn. <short pause> This fight was face to face. And that huge head swivelled on a ball-and-socket joint.

turns.speaker: Skeptic
turns.text: Wait, so those horns were for fighting T. rex?

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.text: And each other. <short pause> Lots of Triceratops frills have healed wounds, likely from locking horns with rivals.

turns.speaker: Skeptic
turns.text: Okay... so did T. rex ever win?

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.text: Oh, it ate plenty. Other skulls have bites that never healed... even on the neck joint.

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.style: building tension, then dark deadpan humor on the jar lid
turns.text: T. rex gripped the frill, pulled... <short pause> and popped the head off to reach the neck meat. Like a jar lid.

turns.speaker: Skeptic
turns.style: horrified, slow disbelief, voice cracking on OFF

turns.speaker: Paleontologist
turns.text: <chuckle> Only after the fight. In Hell Creek, dinner fought back.
